catalog_citation: Tucker, Archibald N. & Margaret A. Bryan. 1966. Linguistic Analyses: The Non-Bantu Languages of North-Eastern Africa (Handbook of African Languages). London: Oxford University Press for the International African Institute. Ch. 1 'The Moru-Mangbetu languages' (heads: Moru-Ma'di, Mangbutu-Efe, Mangbetu, Lendu). Pages read from the Routledge 2017 reprint (Google Books id 3L02DwAAQBAJ) in the copy consulted; 1966 pagination and the chapter-head scope note from scan excerpt of the 1966 printing (archive.org item linguisticanalys0000tuck, controlled lending). Identity of 'Northern LENDU' from Tucker & Bryan 1956, The Non-Bantu Languages of North-Eastern Africa (Handbook of African Languages III), archive.org item nonbantulanguage0000tuck (scan excerpt).
catalog_locator: Ch. 1, sec. 2 'Tone and Stress': 2a Tone (1966 p. 30) and 2b Stress (1966 p. 31) = reprint PT37 (read directly); 2b closes ('In both languages words within a phrase retain their original stress.') and sec. 3 'Word Shape' noun table with rows LENDU (N) / LENDU (S) on 1966 p. 32 = PT38 (read directly). Chapter-head scope note 'LENDU (examples from N. LENDU unless otherwise indicated). Sources: A. N. Tucker, field notes..' c. 1966 p. 27: scan excerpt only. 1956 handbook dialect line: scan excerpt only. Page split 30/31 from the running head 'THE MORU-MANGBETU LANGUAGES 31' (excerpt).
catalog_quote: 2a. Tone. "Tone is both lexical and grammatical. In the MORU-MA'DI languages so far investigated (MORU, MA'DI, LOGO, LUGBARA) and in LENDU, three tone levels have been established, and the same would seem to be the case with MANGBUTU-EFE. According to Larochette, however, there are only two tonemes in MANGBETU-MEJEI. Falling and Rising tones are found only in MANGBETU-MEJE, where they occur in long syllables which are virtually disyllabic. In all languages there are Tone Classes in Nouns and Verbs." 2b. Stress. "Larochette reports a tendency towards stress on the penultimate syllable of a word or phrase in MANGBETU, accompanied sometimes by extra high tone as in nɛkâ- ‘kídriɔ, headache. No such uniformity of stress pattern, however, has been found in the other Language Groups. Even such intimately closely allied languages as MORU and MA'DI have quite different stress behaviour. In MORU stress is on the first syllable of disyllabic words, even when it is a vowel Prefix, e.g. ‘iza, meat; ... In MA'DI, however, stress is on the final vowel ... In both languages words within a phrase retain their original stress." [PT37-PT38] Chapter head [scan excerpt, 1966 printing]: "LENDU (examples from N. LENDU unless otherwise indicated). Sources: A. N. Tucker, field notes". Identity [scan excerpt, 1956 handbook]: "Testament has been published in Northern LENDU. Dialect: Southern LENDU (DRU, NDRU), own name dru-na."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record for Ndrulo, so the work adds new information: a tone statement (three levels) and an explicit absence of any Lendu stress rule, plus the group-level 'no uniform stress pattern found'. Consistent with the Lendu sources already held by the project (Trifkovic 1977a/b: 3-4 level tones + rising; Hartell 1993: high, mid, low, rising), none of which mention stress. The listed open_url (archive.org linguisticanalys0000tuck) itself is lending-locked: and downloads could not be reached by automated download (two attempts), on-item search not reachable by automated download;org FTS APIs. Fresh Google Books search-within calls by automated download were refused (not reachable…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lendu (data from Northern Lendu = Ndrulo) is described as a language with three level tones, lexical and grammatical, with tone classes in nouns and verbs. No word-stress placement is given for Lendu anywhere in the book: the only statement covering it is the group-level negative one that no uniform stress pattern was found in the chapter's groups other than Mangbetu (Lendu being one of the four groups). Full-text probes of the whole book (archive.org FTS and Open Library search-inside: 'LENDU AND stress' size=100, 'stress AND identifier:linguisticanalys0000tuck', '"LENDU (N)" AND stress', 'LENDU AND accent/prominence/unstressed', '"in LENDU" stress') return no fragment in which stress is predicated of Lendu.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Lendu. The Moru (initial) and Ma'di (final) stress rules and the Mangbetu penultimate tendency on the same page concern other languages of the chapter.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan 1966 treat LENDU as one of the four heads of ch. 1 and state that the Lendu examples are 'from N. LENDU unless otherwise indicated'; their noun table on p. 32 has separate rows LENDU (N) and LENDU (S). Northern Lendu is the variety coded as Ndrulo (ISO 639-3 dno 'Lendu North', autonym Ndrǔló; ISO change request 2017-020 held by the project, which separated it from Lendu proper lend1245). So the Lendu tone statement in this book rests primarily on Ndrulo data, while the group-level stress remark covers all Lendu varieties. No Ndrulo-specific stress description is known to exist (Glottolog lists no descriptive references; Kutsch Lojenga's 2013 Ndrulo document is unpublished).

sources.note: Opened: 12 booklet pages of illustrated key words and reading drills, no analytical prose and no statement of the tone inventory. Each vowel or vowel+glide (e, i, o, u, ey, ow, iy, uw..) is drilled unmarked and with tone diacritics: grave (nèné, lùlú, dhùw, bbì, rì), acute (lùlú, ú, éy, ddéy), caron (djǐ, chǒ, lǒ, tdyǒw, ndǔw, lǐy, bǐy, tděy, ěy) and circumflex (dôló); i.e. the Ndrǔló orthography writes at least four tone marks (H acute, L grave, rising caron, falling circumflex) against unmarked vowels (mid, per Kutsch Lojenga 2011 p. 6 for Lendu). First-hand, pedagogical; the tone analysis…
